lesson:
The AI project cycle is a framework consisting of six stages that helps structure how to tackle an artificial intelligence challenge. Visually, the cycle flows from problem scoping through data acquisition, data exploration, modeling, and evaluation, ending with deployment. 

The first stage is problem scoping, which is considered the most important step because it determines success definitions and goals. To ensure completeness, problem scoping utilizes the four Ws framework: Who, What, Where, and Why. "Who" identifies the stakeholders and beneficiaries facing the problem. "What" explores the nature of the problem and the evidence proving it exists. "Where" investigates the context or time perspective in which the problem arises. "Why" establishes the motivation, value proposition, and benefits of solving the problem. 

The second stage is data acquisition, which involves finding and gathering appropriate data for the AI solution. Data can come from internal origin points, such as an e-commerce website tracking user activity, or from external public domain sources and repositories. Examples of external data sources include Kaggle, a platform for AI and data science work; Amazon Web Services (AWS), which provides a registry of open data; the World Bank, which offers national and international data on health, education, and nutrition; and the United States government, which provides population datasets. 

The third stage is data exploration, where data scientists make sense of raw numbers and datasets by viewing them from different perspectives. Visualization tools such as Power BI and Tableau are generally used to transform raw numbers into aggregate charts, graphs, and visual representations, making it easier for humans to identify big-picture characteristics and patterns. 

The fourth stage is modeling, which involves creating a mathematical algorithm based on the data. Artificial intelligence is the overarching concept, with machine learning and deep learning existing inside of it. Machine learning, which will be the primary focus, enables machines to improve through experience, where feeding data into a model acts like an accelerated consumption of past experience. Machine learning models are divided into three main families: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning determines relationships through training on known labeled data, where every data point is categorized by a human with a fixed mark or label. Unsupervised learning involves the machine discovering patterns and correlations independently by traversing large amounts of unlabeled data and grouping similar items together. Reinforcement learning rewards the machine based on actions to help it understand success. Furthermore, supervised learning includes classification and regression techniques. Classification deals with categorical data, which is qualitative and used to predict categories or classes, such as identifying a fox or predicting student grades. Regression deals with numerical data, which is quantitative and used to predict numerical values or measurements, such as housing prices or future student marks. Unsupervised learning includes clustering, which groups unlabeled data into clusters, with K-means clustering serving as a common algorithm example. 

The fifth stage is evaluation, which judges, scores, and assesses the quality, performance, and accuracy of the created model. Each modeling approach has a corresponding evaluation technique. Classification problems use accuracy and the confusion matrix; regression problems use root mean square error; and clustering problems use the silhouette method. 

The sixth and final stage is deployment, where a high-quality model is taken out of the lab and into the real world to solve actual problems in production. Deployment can occur through various mediums, including mobile applications, websites, and cloud servers, allowing real people to take advantage of the completed work.
